analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care for mothers and newborns after birth.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action in the 104th Congress, despite 39 cosponsors including 4 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any health plan that covers childbirth to pay for at least 48 hours of hospital care after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean section, unless the mother and her doctor chose a shorter stay. Plans would also have had to tell enrollees in writing about this coverage. It was introduced in June 1995 and referred to the House Commerce Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: New mothers and their newborns covered by employer or private health plans, who would be guaranteed time in the hospital after birth instead of being discharged within hours. Hospitals also gain, because longer covered stays mean more paid care.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every health plan that covers maternity care to pay for a minimum of 48 hours of inpatient care after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean section, so families are not pressured out of the hospital hours after birth.
Lets a mother leave sooner only if her doctor decides inpatient care is not medically necessary or she requests it, keeping the choice with the patient and physician rather than the insurer.
Requires plans to clearly notify every enrollee in writing about the coverage, and it applied to all plans issued or renewed after a one-year phase-in.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers pay more claims for longer stays, and the employers and plan sponsors who fund coverage bear those added costs, which get passed into premiums for all enrollees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and all premium payers

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises costs for insurers and the employers who fund health plans, and those added claims costs get passed along in premiums to all enrollees, including people who never have a baby.

A federal minimum-stay rule is one-size-fits-all: it applies to every plan nationwide regardless of local practice, and critics of such mandates argue discharge decisions are better left to the mother and her doctor than set by Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: childbirth is common, early discharge of newborns was a widespread complaint, and the bill built in flexibility for mothers who prefer to leave early. The cost is a broad premium increase spread across everyone with private coverage, which is a fair trade for many families but a genuine cost for small employers who buy coverage. The main flaw in how it ended is not the design but that it never moved at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee from July 1995 until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997, never reaching a markup or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Frank Pallone of New Jersey introduced the bill on June 28, 1995, together with Robert Torricelli, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce.
Twelve days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and that was the bill's last recorded action.
The bill attracted 39 cosponsors, 35 Democrats and 4 Republicans, but no committee or subcommittee vote was ever held before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the employers who fund health plans were better off because the bill died, since they avoided paying for the mandated minimum hospital stays; new mothers got no federal guarantee of post-birth hospital time from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers who fund plans

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as lead sponsor.

for.name: Robert Torricelli
for.what_they_did: Joined Pallone in introducing the bill.

for.name: 39 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, 35 Democrats and 4 Republicans.

against.name: Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and never received a markup, subcommittee vote, or floor action during the 104th Congress.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed government-mandated benefit requirements such as minimum hospital stays, which raise claims costs; well documented in coverage of the maternity-stay debate of the mid-1990s.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 39 members including 4 Republicans joined the Democratic sponsor — but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split on the merits is unknown.

industries.note: The bill forces any plan covering maternity care to pay for 48 to 96 hours of post-birth hospital care, raising claims costs. Insurers would lose control over discharge timing, which is where they save money after childbirth.
Longer covered stays mean more paid inpatient days for mothers and newborns. The mandate's goals and the hospital billing interest point the same direction here.
Most workers get coverage through employers, who would absorb the added cost of longer stays through higher premiums.
